fact_rationales.F12: Single S2 and systolic ejection murmur are more typical of truncus arteriosus due to the common arterial trunk, whereas tricuspid atresia would more likely present with different auscultation findings due to the absence of the tricuspid valve.
fact_rationales.F15: Enlarged cardiac silhouette with increased pulmonary vasculature is highly suggestive of truncus arteriosus due to the excessive blood flow to the lungs, whereas tricuspid atresia might show different imaging characteristics due to the underdevelopment of the right ventricle and the presence of atrial septal defect or patent foramen ovale.

fact_rationales.F12: Single S2 and systolic ejection murmur are more typical of Hypoplastic Left Heart Syndrome due to the underdeveloped left heart structures.
fact_rationales.F15: Enlarged cardiac silhouette with increased pulmonary vasculature is highly suggestive of Hypoplastic Left Heart Syndrome due to the increased flow and pressure in the pulmonary circuit.

fact_rationales.F12: Single S2 and systolic ejection murmur are more typical of truncus arteriosus due to the common arterial trunk, whereas tricuspid atresia would more likely present with different auscultation findings.
fact_rationales.F14: Bounding peripheral pulses are more characteristic of truncus arteriosus due to the direct connection between the aorta and pulmonary artery, leading to increased systemic blood flow, whereas tricuspid atresia would not typically present with this finding.
fact_rationales.F15: Enlarged cardiac silhouette with increased pulmonary vasculature is highly suggestive of truncus arteriosus due to the excessive pulmonary blood flow, making it less likely for tricuspid atresia which typically presents with decreased pulmonary blood flow.
fact_rationales.F9: Tachycardia is a nonspecific finding that can be present in both conditions due to distress or decreased cardiac output, thus it does not significantly differentiate between the two.

why.B1.1: Hypoplastic Left Heart Syndrome is a strong candidate due to the single S2, systolic ejection murmur, and enlarged cardiac silhouette with increased pulmonary vasculature, which are typical of underdeveloped left heart structures and increased flow and pressure in the pulmonary circuit.
why.B2.3: Patent ductus arteriosus is a possible explanation for the enlarged cardiac silhouette with increased pulmonary vasculature due to the left-to-right shunt, but it less specifically accounts for the single S2 and systolic ejection murmur compared to Truncus Arteriosus and Hypoplastic Left Heart Syndrome.
why.B4.4: Truncus Arteriosus best explains the single S2, systolic ejection murmur, and enlarged cardiac silhouette with increased pulmonary vasculature due to the common arterial trunk and excessive blood flow to the lungs.

fact_rationales.F12: A single S2 and systolic ejection murmur can be found in various cardiac defects, but are more typical of ventricular septal defects.
fact_rationales.F15: An enlarged cardiac silhouette with increased pulmonary vasculature is highly suggestive of a left-to-right shunt, such as patent ductus arteriosus.
